title: Saluti e Presentazioni
subtitle: Greet people and introduce yourself — and know when to use tu or Lei.
objectives: Greet someone and say goodbye at any time of day
Introduce yourself and ask someone's name
Choose between the informal tu and the formal Lei

content.intro: Every conversation in Italian starts with a greeting — and the greeting you choose already signals how formal the conversation will be.
content.explanation:
Italian has time-of-day greetings (buongiorno, buonasera) that work in both formal and informal situations, and an all-purpose informal ciao used only with people you're on first-name terms with — friends, family, children, and often colleagues your own age. Salve sits in between: a polite, neutral greeting safe for someone you don't know well.

Italian also has two ways to say “you”: tu (informal, singular) and Lei (formal, singular — note the capital L, and that it takes third-person verb forms, the same as lui/lei). Use Lei with strangers, older people, doctors, officials, and anyone in a professional context until they invite you to use tu (diamoci del tu, “let's use tu with each other”).

rules.heading: a) Greetings by time and formality
rules.body:
• Buongiorno — good morning / good day (formal or informal, until mid-afternoon)
  • Buonasera — good evening (formal or informal, from mid-afternoon)
  • Buonanotte — good night (only when leaving/going to bed, never as a greeting on arrival)
  • Ciao — hi / bye (informal only, any time)
  • Salve — hello (neutral, safe with strangers)
  • Arrivederci — goodbye (formal-safe); ArrivederLa is the fully formal version

rules.heading: b) Asking and giving names
rules.body:
• Informal: Come ti chiami? (What's your name?) → Mi chiamo Marco.
  • Formal: Come si chiama? → Mi chiamo Marco. (the answer doesn't change)
  • Piacere — “pleasure [to meet you]”, said by both people when introduced

rules.heading: c) Tu vs. Lei
rules.body:
• Tu: friends, family, children, peers — Tu come stai?
  • Lei: strangers, elders, professional settings — Lei come sta?
  • Lei uses third-person singular verb forms, the same ones used for lui/lei (he/she)

examples.it: Mi chiamo Giulia. E tu, come ti chiami?
examples.en: My name is Giulia. And you, what's your name?
I'm well, thank you. And you? (formal)

commonMistakes.right: Ciao, come stai? / Buongiorno, come sta?
commonMistakes.why: Ciao is informal, so it pairs with the informal stai — mixing ciao with the formal sta is inconsistent.
Buonanotte is only for leaving or going to bed, never for greeting someone on arrival.

commonMistakes.right: Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama?
commonMistakes.why: Ti chiami is the tu-form (2nd person: you call yourself); ti chiama mixes tu with a 3rd-person verb ending.

items.prompt: You meet your boss for the first time this morning. What do you say?
items.explanation: Buongiorno is the safe, formal-appropriate morning greeting for someone you don't know well.

items.prompt: You're leaving your friend's house late at night.
items.explanation: Buonanotte is used when leaving or going to bed, paired here with the informal ciao since it's a friend.

items.prompt: Which pronoun goes with a stranger you're asking for directions?
items.explanation: Lei is the formal singular "you", the safe default with strangers.
Chiami is the informal tu-form of chiamarsi.
Sta is the formal Lei-form of stare, matching buonasera used formally here.
Ciao is informal, so it should pair with the informal stai, not the formal sta.

items.incorrect: Buonanotte! (greeting a colleague who just arrived)
items.explanation: Buonanotte is never used to greet someone arriving — only when leaving or going to sleep.

items.prompt: You want to say goodbye to a close friend.
items.explanation: Ciao works both as hello and goodbye between people on first-name terms.

items.prompt: Your elderly neighbor, whom you barely know, greets you first thing in the morning. How do you reply?
items.explanation: Buongiorno is the safe, formal-appropriate morning greeting.

items.prompt: Which word means "pleasure to meet you"?
items.explanation: Piacere is said by both people when they're introduced.

items.prompt: You want to ask a stranger's name formally.
items.explanation: Come si chiama is the formal way to ask someone's name.

items.prompt: Which greeting is safe with someone you've just met and don't know how formal to be?
items.explanation: Salve is neutral and polite, a safe default with strangers.

items.prompt: It's 6pm and you're arriving at a business meeting. What do you say?
items.explanation: Buonasera is used from mid-afternoon on, for both formal and informal arrivals.

items.prompt: How do you say goodbye formally to your doctor?
items.explanation: Arrivederci is the formal-safe way to say goodbye.
Buongiorno is the standard formal morning greeting.
Ciao is informal, safe for a friend you'll see again.
Mi chiamo (I call myself) is the answer, whichever way the question was asked.

items.prompt: — Come si chiama? — Mi ___ signor Rossi.
items.explanation: The answer is always mi chiamo, even after the formal question.
Buonanotte is used specifically when going to bed.

items.prompt: — Buonasera, come ___? (formal, to your boss) — Bene, grazie.
items.explanation: Sta is the formal Lei-form of stare.

items.prompt: — Ciao, come ___? (informal, to your friend) — Sto benissimo!
items.explanation: Stai is the informal tu-form of stare, matching the informal ciao.

items.statement: Ciao can be used with your bank manager the first time you meet them.
items.explanation: Ciao is informal-only; use Buongiorno or Salve with someone you don't know well.

items.statement: Buonanotte is used to greet someone arriving late in the evening.
items.explanation: Buonanotte is only for leaving or going to bed — a late arrival still gets buonasera.

items.statement: Lei is written with a capital L when it means the formal "you".
items.explanation: Capitalizing Lei distinguishes formal "you" from lei meaning "she" in writing.

items.statement: The answer to both "Come ti chiami?" and "Come si chiama?" is "Mi chiamo...".
items.explanation: The question changes with formality, but the answer form stays the same.

items.statement: Buongiorno can only be used in formal situations.
items.explanation: Buongiorno works in both formal and informal contexts.

items.statement: Lei (formal you) takes the same verb form as lui/lei (he/she).
items.explanation: Formal Lei uses third-person singular verb forms, the same as lui/lei.

items.incorrect: Buongiorno! (said to a friend leaving your house at midnight)
items.explanation: Leaving at midnight calls for buonanotte, not buongiorno.
Mixing the formal piacere di conoscerLa with informal ciao is inconsistent — a formal greeting should close formally too.

items.incorrect: Come si chiama? Mi chiami Paolo.
answer: Come si chiama? Mi chiamo Paolo.
items.explanation: The reply always uses mi chiamo (I call myself), not mi chiami.

items.incorrect: Buonanotte, buongiorno a tutti! (arriving at the office in the morning)
items.explanation: Buonanotte is never used on arrival, only when leaving.
The tu-form ends in -i (chiami), not -a (chiama), which is the lui/lei form.

items.incorrect: Ciao, come si chiama? (to your best friend)
items.explanation: Ciao signals an informal context, so it should pair with the informal ti chiami, not the formal si chiama.

summary: Buongiorno/buonasera work formally or informally; ciao is informal-only; buonanotte is for leaving, not arriving.
Come ti chiami? (informal) vs. Come si chiama? (formal) — the answer, mi chiamo..., stays the same.
Use tu with people you're close to; use Lei with strangers, elders and professional contacts.
